claim: Narration renders a character's opinion in that character's own words without quotation marks, so the verdict sounds like the narrator's until it turns.
example: His character was decided. He was the proudest, most disagreeable man in the world, and every body hoped that he would never come there again.

claim: Leans heavily on negation and litotes, praising or blaming by denying the opposite.
example: Elizabeth remained with no very cordial feelings towards him.

claim: Prefers abstract Latinate nouns for feelings and conduct over physical description.
example: Attention, forbearance, patience with Darcy, was injury to Wickham.

claim: Builds long sentences out of semicolon-joined clauses that each add a fresh qualification.
example: They were in fact very fine ladies; not deficient in good humour when they were pleased, nor in the power of being agreeable where they chose it; but proud and conceited.

claim: Marks spoken stress with italics on single pronouns or small words.
example: _You_ are dancing with the only handsome girl in the room,

claim: Gives each speaker a recognisable verbal tic, such as stock phrases, exclamations or dash-broken gushing.
example: My dear, dear Lydia! she cried: "This is delightful indeed!--She will be married!--I shall see her again!

claim: Tags dialogue with varied speech verbs plus a manner adverb or phrase.
Lists money, income and fortune as exact figures alongside character traits.
example: had a fortune of twenty thousand pounds, were in the habit of spending more than they ought

claim: Ends a long passage of report with a short, flat sentence that undercuts it.
example: Sir William did not say much. He was storing his memory with anecdotes and noble names.

claim: Never uses contractions in narration, and almost never in the speech of educated characters.
Almost never describes landscape, weather or objects in sensory detail for their own sake.
Never uses colons or parentheses as ordinary narrative punctuation.
Never lets the narrator address the reader as "you" or step forward as "I".
Takes the reader into confidence with dry general verdicts on human conduct, delivered as settled fact.
example: Such amiable qualities must speak for themselves.

claim: Trusts the reader to catch irony without signalling it, leaving self-condemning speeches unanswered.
example: I have more than once observed to Lady Catherine, that her charming daughter seemed born to be a duchess,

claim: Shifts freely between a cool outside summary and one character's private reasoning within a paragraph.
example: Elizabeth however did not chuse to take the hint, being well aware that a serious dispute must be the consequence of any reply.

claim: The humour is deadpan anticlimax, where a sentence builds a serious frame and then drops in a trivial particular.
example: and had even vouchsafed to suggest some herself,--some shelves in the closets up stairs.

claim: Characters score off each other with paradox and symmetrical reversals in dialogue.
example: Your mother will never see you again if you do _not_ marry Mr. Collins, and I will never see you again if you _do_.

claim: Exaggeration is placed in a character's mouth and allowed to run until it exposes itself.
example: He walked here, and he walked there, fancying himself so very great! Not handsome enough to dance with!

claim: Long narrative paragraphs alternate with runs of very short dialogue lines, many of them one sentence.
Sentences often grow by triads and balanced pairs, three parallel items or an antithetical "not this but that."
example: for he was discovered to be proud, to be above his company, and above being pleased;

claim: Inside excited speech, dashes break sentences into breathless fragments.
example: Heaven forbid!--_That_ would be the greatest misfortune of all!--To find a man agreeable whom one is determined to hate!|yes
